_comment: Preguntas ORIGINALES tipo NIE del capítulo 2.7. No son preguntas reales del examen. Comprueba con tu edición 2027.

questions.scenario: ROSS stands on the other side of a busy road and shouts at PAGE that he is going to 'batter him next week'. PAGE is frightened. Has ROSS committed an assault?
options: No, because PAGE did not apprehend the application of immediate unlawful force
Yes, because PAGE was frightened
Yes, because threats are always assaults
No, because words can never amount to an assault
explanations: Fear alone is not enough; the force must be apprehended as immediate.
Incorrect: the threat must be of immediate force.
Incorrect: words (or silence) can amount to an assault (R v Ireland).

questions.scenario: FRANKS makes a series of silent telephone calls at night to a former colleague, who becomes terrified that he is about to come round. Which of the following is correct?
options: Silence can never be an assault
This can only be harassment
Silent calls can amount to an assault if the victim apprehends immediate unlawful force
This is a battery
explanations: Harassment may also apply, but assault is possible.

questions.scenario: Which statement best describes a battery?
options: Causing someone to fear immediate unlawful force
The intentional or reckless application of unlawful force to another
Causing actual bodily harm
Wounding another person

questions.scenario: HAYES punches a woman who is holding her baby. She drops the baby, who is injured. In relation to the baby, which of the following is correct?
options: There is no battery because HAYES did not touch the baby
HAYES has only committed an assault
The mother is liable for dropping the baby
A battery can be committed indirectly, so HAYES may have committed a battery on the baby
explanations: Incorrect: force can be applied indirectly.

questions.scenario: Common assault and battery are charged under which provision, and how are they tried?
options: s. 47 OAPA 1861 – either way
s. 18 OAPA 1861 – indictable only
s. 39 Criminal Justice Act 1988 – summary only
s. 89 Police Act 1996 – either way

questions.scenario: CLARK pushes MILLS, intending only to push her. MILLS falls and suffers a broken wrist. CLARK did not foresee any injury. Considering s. 47 OAPA 1861, which is correct?
options: CLARK may be guilty because the mens rea of s. 47 is that of the assault/battery only
CLARK is not guilty because he did not foresee any harm
CLARK must be charged with s. 18
CLARK is only guilty of battery because the harm was accidental
explanations: Correct: R v Savage; DPP v Parmenter.
Incorrect: foresight of harm is not required.
s. 47 applies if ABH is caused.

questions.scenario: Which of the following is LEAST likely to amount to 'actual bodily harm'?
options: Cutting off a substantial amount of a person's hair
A recognised psychiatric injury
Bruising to the arm
A brief feeling of fear and panic
explanations: Correct: mere emotions are not ABH.

questions.scenario: GREEN punches WHITE. WHITE's skin is unbroken but his collarbone is fractured. Has GREEN 'wounded' WHITE for the purposes of s. 20?
options: Yes, because a fracture is a wound
No, because a wound requires both layers of skin to be broken
Yes, because any injury is a wound
No, because a punch can never cause a wound
explanations: Correct: JCC v Eisenhower (1984) – but GBH may be inflicted.
Incorrect: a punch can split skin.

questions.scenario: A punch splits the inside of a victim's lip, causing bleeding. Which statement is correct?
options: This can be a wound because the continuity of the inner skin of the mouth is broken
This cannot be a wound because the skin outside is intact
This is only battery
This is automatically GBH
explanations: Incorrect: inner skin of the mouth counts.
It may be more than battery.

questions.scenario: What is meant by 'grievous bodily harm'?
options: Any injury requiring hospital treatment
Any wound
Really serious harm, assessed considering all the injuries and the victim
Harm that lasts more than a week
explanations: Correct: DPP v Smith (1961); R v Bollom (2003).

questions.scenario: For an offence under s. 20 OAPA 1861, what must the defendant have foreseen?
options: That GBH would result
That some physical harm, albeit minor, might result
That death might result
Nothing – it is strict liability

questions.scenario: HOLT causes a former partner serious psychiatric illness through months of threatening behaviour, without ever touching her or making her fear immediate force. Can HOLT be guilty of 'inflicting' GBH under s. 20?
options: No, because 'inflict' requires an assault
No, because psychiatric injury is never GBH
Only under s. 47
Yes – inflicting GBH does not require an assault and serious psychiatric injury can be GBH

questions.scenario: During an arrest, DEAN stabs the arresting officer in the arm, intending to escape but not to cause serious harm. Which offence is most appropriate?
options: s. 20 only, because he did not intend GBH
Common assault
s. 18 – wounding with intent to resist or prevent lawful apprehension
s. 47 only
explanations: s. 18 also covers intent to resist arrest.
Too low – there is a wound.
questions.manualRef: Blackstone's 2027 · 2.7 · s. 18 – intent to resist apprehension

questions.scenario: Which of the following is correct about s. 18 OAPA 1861?
options: It is a specific intent offence, triable only on indictment, with a maximum of life imprisonment
It is a basic intent offence
It is triable either way
It requires only recklessness as to GBH

questions.scenario: Two friends have a 'play fight' with no intention to hurt, and one suffers a broken arm. Considering consent, which is correct?
options: Consent can never be a defence to ABH or worse
Consent is only possible in boxing
Consent is irrelevant to all assaults
Rough horseplay is a recognised exception where genuine consent (or belief in it) may be a defence

questions.scenario: A group engage in sado-masochistic activities in private, all adults consenting, causing wounds. According to R v Brown (1993)…
options: their consent is a defence
consent is not a defence to ABH or wounding in these circumstances
only the person who caused the wounds is liable for battery
no offence is committed in private

questions.scenario: Under the Domestic Abuse Act 2021, s. 71, which is correct?
options: Consent to serious harm for sexual gratification is not a defence to ABH or more serious offences
Consent is now always a defence
It only applies to married couples
It only applies to battery
explanations: It applies to ABH and above.

questions.scenario: In England, a mother smacks her 8-year-old son, causing bruising that lasts several days. Which is correct?
options: The defence of reasonable punishment is available
No offence because she is a parent
The defence of reasonable punishment is not available because the harm amounts to ABH
Reasonable punishment applies to all assaults
explanations: Correct: Children Act 2004, s. 58 – only common assault/battery.
questions.manualRef: Blackstone's 2027 · 2.7 · Reasonable punishment – s. 58 Children Act 2004

questions.scenario: JAMES genuinely but mistakenly believes that a man reaching into his pocket is about to stab him, and punches him. In self-defence, how is the force judged?
options: Against the true facts only
By whether it was reasonable in the circumstances as JAMES believed them to be
By whether the victim was armed
It is never reasonable to strike first
explanations: Correct: CJIA 2008, s. 76 (unless the mistake was due to voluntary intoxication).

questions.scenario: In a 'householder case' under s. 76 CJIA 2008, which statement is correct?
options: Any force is lawful
Force must always be proportionate
Only force with a weapon is allowed
Disproportionate force may be reasonable, but grossly disproportionate force is not

questions.scenario: WEBB, drunk, mistakenly believes he is being attacked and hits an innocent person. Can he rely on his mistaken belief?
options: Yes, any honest belief counts
Yes, if the mistake was reasonable
No – a mistaken belief attributable to voluntary intoxication cannot be relied on
Only if he is a householder
explanations: Not if due to voluntary intoxication.
The test isn't reasonableness of the mistake.

questions.scenario: Under the Assaults on Emergency Workers (Offences) Act 2018, which is correct?
options: It covers common assault/battery on an emergency worker acting in the exercise of functions, and makes the emergency-worker status an aggravating factor for other offences
It only protects police officers
It replaces s. 18
It applies only when the worker is off duty
explanations: It covers other workers too (fire, ambulance, NHS, prison…).

questions.scenario: TODD, who is not under arrest, deliberately stands in a doorway to stop PC LANE entering to save a life. Which offence is most relevant under the Police Act 1996, s. 89?
options: Assaulting a constable
Threats to kill
s. 47 ABH
Wilfully obstructing a constable in the execution of their duty

questions.scenario: NASH sends a message to his ex-partner: 'I will kill you when I find you', intending that she believes he will do it. He has no intention of killing her. Which is correct?
options: No offence, because he did not intend to kill
He may commit threats to kill because he intended her to fear the threat would be carried out
Threats to kill requires the threat to be made face to face
It is only an assault
explanations: Intention to kill is not required.
There is no apprehension of immediate force.

questions.scenario: A threat to kill can be made in relation to…
options: the person who receives it or a third person
only the person who receives the threat
only a police officer
only a child
explanations: Correct: e.g. threatening to kill someone's child.

questions.scenario: During an argument, KANE puts his hands around his partner's neck for a few seconds. She has no visible injury. Considering the offence of non-fatal strangulation (Serious Crime Act 2015, s. 75A), which is correct?
options: No offence without injury
It only applies to strangers
The offence can be committed without any injury being caused
It requires an intention to kill

questions.scenario: Which of the following is an assault rather than a battery?
options: Spitting on someone
Raising a baseball bat at someone who believes he is about to be hit
Pushing someone over
Throwing water over someone

questions.scenario: A doctor performs properly conducted surgery with the patient's consent, causing a large wound. Why is this not s. 20?
options: Because doctors cannot commit offences
Because the wound was small
Because surgery is strict liability
Because surgery is a recognised exception where consent is effective

questions.scenario: Which offence requires proof of intent to cause GBH (or to resist lawful apprehension)?
BELL throws a stone at a crowd, aware it might hit someone. It strikes a man, causing a deep cut. Which best describes BELL's mens rea for s. 20?
options: He was reckless as to causing some harm, which is enough for 'maliciously'
He needed to intend a wound
He needed to know who he would hit
s. 20 has no mens rea
